title: Money Basics
description: Needs vs. wants, where money comes from, and why your paycheck is smaller than you expected.

lessons.title: Needs vs. wants
body: A need is something you must have to live, work, or stay safe. Think food, a place to live, basic clothes, and getting to work or school.
A want is something that makes life more fun or easier, but you could live without it. Think concert tickets, a new game, or name-brand sneakers.
The tricky part: the same thing can be both. You need shoes. You want the $180 pair. The basic version is the need; the upgrade is the want.
lessons.keyIdea: Ask: "What happens if I don't buy this?" If the answer is "not much," it's a want.
lessons.example: Phone service you need for work = need. The newest phone model when yours works fine = want.

lessons.title: Where money comes from
body: Income is money coming in. For most teens that's a part-time job, an allowance, gifts, or side gigs like babysitting, mowing lawns, or tutoring.
Some income is steady (a job with set hours). Some is irregular (birthday money, summer gigs). Steady income is easier to plan around.
When income is irregular, plan your budget using the lowest month you expect. Treat extra money as a bonus for saving.
lessons.keyIdea: You can only spend money once. Knowing how much comes in is step one of every budget.
lessons.example: You earn about $150 a month babysitting, but some months only $80. Plan as if it's $80, and save anything over that.

lessons.title: Gross pay vs. net pay
body: Gross pay is what you earn before anything is taken out: hourly wage × hours worked.
Net pay ("take-home pay") is what actually lands in your bank account after taxes and other deductions.
Your first paycheck might feel small. That's normal! Always budget with net pay, because that's the money you can actually spend.
lessons.keyIdea: Gross = before taxes. Net = after taxes. Budget with net.
lessons.example: You work 20 hours at $15/hour. Gross pay = 20 × $15 = $300. After taxes you might take home about $235.

lessons.title: What gets taken out of a paycheck
body: Federal income tax pays for national things like roads and the military. How much depends on how much you earn. Many teens with small incomes get some or all of it back as a tax refund.
State income tax works the same way for your state. Some states don't have one.
FICA is Social Security (6.2%) plus Medicare (1.45%). These pay for retirement and health care for older adults. You don't get these back.
When you start a job you fill out a W-4 form. It tells your employer how much federal tax to hold back.
lessons.keyIdea: Your pay stub lists every deduction. Read it the first time so nothing surprises you.
lessons.example: In the Paycheck calculator, try changing the hours to see how each deduction grows with your pay.

lessons.title: Every choice has a cost
body: Opportunity cost is what you give up when you choose one thing over another. Spending $60 on a game means that $60 can't go toward your car fund.
Try the 24-hour rule: when you want something that isn't a need, wait a day. If you still want it tomorrow, it might be worth it.
Another trick: turn prices into hours of work. If you earn $12 an hour, $90 sneakers cost you 7.5 hours of work.
lessons.keyIdea: Before buying, ask: "What else could this money do for me?"
lessons.example: A $6 drink every school day is about $120 a month. That's almost 10 hours of work at $12/hour.

choices: A new phone case with your favorite team on it
Gas to drive to your job
practice.explanation: Gas gets you to work, and work is how you earn money. The others are nice to have, but you could live without them.

practice.prompt: You work 15 hours at $12 an hour. What is your gross pay?
practice.explanation: Gross pay = hours × hourly wage = 15 × $12 = $180. That's before any taxes come out.

practice.prompt: Your gross pay is $250. Your pay stub shows $41 taken out for taxes. What is your net pay?
practice.explanation: Net pay = gross pay − deductions = $250 − $41 = $209. This is what you can actually spend.

practice.prompt: Social Security takes 6.2% of your gross pay. If you earn $300 gross, how much goes to Social Security?
Your income changes month to month (some months $200, some months $120). Which amount should you build your budget on?
choices: Don't make a budget until income is steady
practice.explanation: Plan with the lowest month you expect. Then you never come up short, and extra months become bonus savings.
practice.reviewed: Picks the lowest of the listed amounts; no calculation.

practice.prompt: You earn $12 an hour. How many hours of work does a $90 pair of sneakers cost you?
practice.explanation: $90 ÷ $12 per hour = 7.5 hours of work. Thinking in hours makes prices feel more real.

choices: Your pay after taxes and deductions
quiz.explanation: Net pay is your take-home pay: what's left after taxes and other deductions.

quiz.prompt: You need shoes for your job. Which choice keeps it a need and not a want?
choices: A basic, comfortable $55 pair that meets the dress code
Two pairs so you have options
quiz.explanation: The basic pair covers the need. Anything fancier is the "want" part of the purchase.

quiz.prompt: You work 18 hours at $14 an hour. What is your gross pay?
Medicare takes 1.45% of gross pay. About how much is that on a $400 paycheck?

choices: The sales tax on a purchase
What you give up when you choose one thing over another
The cost of a job interview
quiz.explanation: Every dollar can only be spent once. The thing you didn't get is the opportunity cost.

quiz.prompt: Which form tells your employer how much federal tax to hold back from your pay?
quiz.explanation: You fill out a W-4 when you start a job. Your employer uses it to figure out federal tax withholding.

quiz.prompt: You buy a $5 drink every school day. With about 20 school days in a month, how much is that per month?
quiz.explanation: $5 × 20 days = $100 a month. Small daily buys add up fast.

quiz.prompt: Which deductions do you usually not get back as a refund?
quiz.explanation: Income tax can be partly refunded if too much was held back. FICA (Social Security + Medicare) is not refunded.

flashcards.back: Something you must have to live, work, or stay safe (food, housing, basic clothes, getting to work).
Something nice to have that you could live without (games, concerts, name brands).
What you earn before taxes: hourly wage × hours worked.
Take-home pay: what's left after taxes and deductions. Budget with this number.
Social Security (6.2%) + Medicare (1.45%) taken from each paycheck.
What you give up when you choose to spend money on something else.
